1 - Problem Statement¶

Business Context¶

Business communities in the United States are facing high demand for human resources, but one of the constant challenges is identifying and attracting the right talent, which is perhaps the most important element in remaining competitive. Companies in the United States look for hard-working, talented, and qualified individuals both locally as well as abroad.

The Immigration and Nationality Act (INA) of the US permits foreign workers to come to the United States to work on either a temporary or permanent basis. The act also protects US workers against adverse impacts on their wages or working conditions by ensuring US employers' compliance with statutory requirements when they hire foreign workers to fill workforce shortages. The immigration programs are administered by the Office of Foreign Labor Certification (OFLC).

OFLC processes job certification applications for employers seeking to bring foreign workers into the United States and grants certifications in those cases where employers can demonstrate that there are not sufficient US workers available to perform the work at wages that meet or exceed the wage paid for the occupation in the area of intended employment.

Objective¶

In FY 2016, the OFLC processed 775,979 employer applications for 1,699,957 positions for temporary and permanent labor certifications. This was a nine percent increase in the overall number of processed applications from the previous year. The process of reviewing every case is becoming a tedious task as the number of applicants is increasing every year.

The increasing number of applicants every year calls for a Machine Learning based solution that can help in shortlisting the candidates having higher chances of VISA approval. OFLC has hired the firm EasyVisa for data-driven solutions. You as a data scientist at EasyVisa have to analyze the data provided and, with the help of a classification model:

  • Facilitate the process of visa approvals.
  • Recommend a suitable profile for the applicants for whom the visa should be certified or denied based on the drivers that significantly influence the case status.

Data Description¶

The data contains the different attributes of employee and the employer. The detailed data dictionary is given below.

  • case_id: ID of each visa application
  • continent: Information of continent the employee
  • education_of_employee: Information of education of the employee
  • has_job_experience: Does the employee has any job experience? Y= Yes; N = No
  • requires_job_training: Does the employee require any job training? Y = Yes; N = No
  • no_of_employees: Number of employees in the employer's company
  • yr_of_estab: Year in which the employer's company was established
  • region_of_employment: Information of foreign worker's intended region of employment in the US.
  • prevailing_wage: Average wage paid to similarly employed workers in a specific occupation in the area of intended employment. The purpose of the prevailing wage is to ensure that the foreign worker is not underpaid compared to other workers offering the same or similar service in the same area of employment.
  • unit_of_wage: Unit of prevailing wage. Values include Hourly, Weekly, Monthly, and Yearly.
  • full_time_position: Is the position of work full-time? Y = Full Time Position; N = Part Time Position
  • case_status: Flag indicating if the Visa was certified or denied

def filter_malloc_warnings(original_write, message):
    if "MallocStackLogging" not in message:
        original_write(message)

original_stderr = sys.stderr.write
sys.stderr.write = partial(filter_malloc_warnings, original_stderr)

5 - Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)¶

Plot Functions¶

In [29]:
def plot_numerical_distributions(data, numerical_features, hue=None, figsize=(16, 12), dpi=100, bins=30, palette="viridis", plot_style="whitegrid", show_median=True):
    
    # Set style and palette
    sns.set_style(plot_style)
    sns.set_palette(palette)
    
    # Calculate grid dimensions
    n_cols = 2
    n_rows = (len(numerical_features) // n_cols) + (1 if len(numerical_features) % n_cols else 0)
    
    # Create figure
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=figsize, dpi=dpi)
    fig.suptitle('Distribution Analysis', y=1.02, fontsize=16, fontweight='bold')
    
    for i, feature in enumerate(numerical_features, 1):
        ax = plt.subplot(n_rows, n_cols, i)
        
        # Plot histogram with KDE
        sns.histplot(data=data, x=feature, hue=hue, kde=True, bins=bins, edgecolor='white', linewidth=0.5, stat='count', alpha=0.7)
        
        # Add median line
        if show_median:
            median = data[feature].median()
            ax.axvline(median, color='red', linestyle='--', linewidth=1.5)
            x_offset = 0.02 * (ax.get_xlim()[1] - ax.get_xlim()[0])  # 2% of x-axis range
            ax.text(median + x_offset, ax.get_ylim()[1]*0.9, f'Median: {median:.1f}', color='red', va='top')
        
        # Formatting
        ax.set_title(f'{feature} Distribution', pad=10)
        ax.set_xlabel('')
        ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
    
    plt.tight_layout()
    
    return fig
In [30]:
def plot_numerical_boxplots(data, numerical_features, figsize=(16, 12), palette="viridis", plot_style="whitegrid", showfliers=True, notch=False, orient="v", hue=None):

    # Set visual style
    sns.set_style(plot_style)
    plt.rcParams['font.size'] = 12
    
    # Calculate grid dimensions
    n_cols = 2
    n_rows = (len(numerical_features) // n_cols) + (1 if len(numerical_features) % n_cols else 0)
    
    # Initialize figure
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=figsize, dpi=100, layout="constrained")
    fig.suptitle('Numerical Features Distribution Analysis (Boxplots)', fontsize=18, fontweight='bold', y=1.02)
    
    # Create subplots
    for idx, feature in enumerate(numerical_features, start=1):
        ax = fig.add_subplot(n_rows, n_cols, idx)
        
        # Plot boxplot with enhanced aesthetics
        sns.boxplot(
            data=data,
            x=feature if orient == "v" else None,
            y=None if orient == "v" else feature,
            hue=hue,
            palette=palette,
            width=0.6,
            showfliers=showfliers,
            notch=notch,
            linewidth=1.5,
            fliersize=3,
            saturation=0.8
        )
        

        
        # Add mean marker
        mean_val = data[feature].mean()
        if orient == "v":
            ax.axvline(mean_val, color='red', linestyle='--', linewidth=1.2, label=f'Mean: {mean_val:.1f}')
        else:
            ax.axhline(mean_val, color='red', linestyle='--', linewidth=1.2, label=f'Mean: {mean_val:.1f}')
        ax.legend(loc='upper right')
        
        # Format subplot
        ax.set_title(f'{feature} Distribution', pad=12, fontweight='semibold')
        if orient == "v":
            ax.set_ylabel('Value', fontsize=12)
        else:
            ax.set_xlabel('Value', fontsize=12)
        ax.grid(visible=True, alpha=0.2, axis='y' if orient == "v" else 'x')
        
        # Remove top/right spines
        sns.despine(ax=ax, top=True, right=True)
    
    # Add figure caption
    caption = "Note: Red dashed line shows mean value. Box shows IQR (25th-75th percentile)"
    if showfliers:
        caption += ". Points show outliers."
    if hue:
        caption += f" Grouped by {hue}."
    fig.text(
        0.5, 0.01,
        caption,
        ha='center',
        fontsize=12,
        color='dimgray'
    )
    
    return fig
In [31]:
def plot_categorical_distributions(data, categorical_features, hue="",figsize=(16, 18), palette="viridis", plot_style="whitegrid", annotate=True, rotate_labels=False):
    # Set visual style
    sns.set_style(plot_style)
    plt.rcParams['font.size'] = 12
    
    # Calculate grid dimensions
    n_cols = 2
    n_rows = (len(categorical_features) // n_cols) + (1 if len(categorical_features) % n_cols else 0)
    
    # Initialize figure
    fig = plt.figure(figsize=figsize, dpi=100, layout="constrained")
    fig.suptitle('Distribution Analysis', fontsize=18, fontweight='bold', y=1.02)
    
    # Create subplots
    for idx, feature in enumerate(categorical_features, start=1):
        ax = fig.add_subplot(n_rows, n_cols, idx)
        
        # Plot with improved aesthetics
        if hue:
            # If hue is provided, use countplot with hue
            plot = sns.countplot(data=data, x=feature, hue=hue, palette=palette, edgecolor='black', linewidth=0.5, alpha=0.85)
        else:
            # If no hue is provided, use countplot without hue
            plot = sns.countplot(data=data, x=feature, palette=palette, edgecolor='black', linewidth=0.5, alpha=0.85, order=data[feature].value_counts().index)  # Sort by frequency
        
        # Add count annotations
        if annotate:
            for p in ax.patches:
                ax.annotate(
                    f'{p.get_height():,.0f}',
                    (p.get_x() + p.get_width() / 2., p.get_height()),
                    ha='center', va='center',
                    xytext=(0, 5),
                    textcoords='offset points',
                    fontsize=10
                )
        
        # Rotate labels if needed
        if rotate_labels:
            plt.setp(ax.get_xticklabels(), rotation=45, ha='right')
        
        # Format subplot
        ax.set_title(f'{feature} Distribution', pad=12, fontweight='semibold')
        ax.set_xlabel('')
        ax.set_ylabel('Count', fontsize=12)
        ax.grid(visible=True, alpha=0.2, axis='y')
        
        # Remove top/right spines
        sns.despine(ax=ax, top=True, right=True)
        
    return fig

Bivariate Analysis Observations (Numerical Variables vs Case Status)¶

Number of Employees vs Case Status¶

  • Companies with fewer employees have a higher rate of certification. The concentration of Certified cases is heaviest in firms with small to medium workforce sizes.

Year of Establishment vs. Case Status¶

  • Companies established between 1900 and 2000 dominate Certified cases.
  • Companies stablished after 2000, have a more mixed case outcome.

Prevailing Wage vs. Case Status¶

  • Certified cases are spread across a broad range of prevailing wages, but a strong cluster appears in the lower-to-mid wage range.
  • Denied cases do not appear to be heavily concentrated in any specific wage range.
  • Higher prevailing wages show fewer denied cases overall.

Bivariate Analysis Observations (Categorical Variables vs Case Status)¶

Continent vs Case Status¶

  • Asia has the highest volume of applications, with Certified cases outnumbering Denied.
  • Africa and South America show a higher proportion of Denied cases relative to their total applications.
  • Europe has a high certification rate, while North America has a more balanced split between Certified and Denied cases.

Education Level vs Case Status¶

  • Master’s and Doctorate degrees see higher certification rates, indicating a possible preference for applicants with advanced education.
  • High School education shows more Denied cases than Certified, suggesting lower approval chances for less-educated applicants.
  • Bachelor’s degrees have a substantial number of both Certified and Denied cases, but Certification remains dominant.

Job Experience vs Case Status¶

  • Applicants with job experience have significantly more Certified cases, indicating that prior experience may boost approval chances.
  • Applicants without experience show a more balanced distribution, meaning a lack of experience may contribute to increased denials.

Requires Job Training vs Case Status¶

  • Positions that do not require training have significantly more Certified cases.
  • Positions that require training are more likely to be denied.

Region of Employment vs. Case Status¶

  • The West region has a disproportionately high number of Denied cases, compared to other regions.
  • Midwest and South exhibit more Certified applications, implying a higher approval trend in these areas.
  • The Northeast region has a significant number of Denied cases, but Certified ones still dominate.

Wage Unit vs. Case Status¶

  • Yearly wage earners are certified the most—suggesting annual salary structures may influence positive case outcomes.
  • Hourly wage applicants see a higher rate of Denied cases, indicating a potential disadvantage for workers paid by the hour.

Full-time vs. Case Status¶

  • Full Time positions are certified 66%.
  • Non-full-time positions are certified 68%
  • There seems that there is the same probability to be certified for Full time and part time positions.

6 - Data Pre-processing¶

Outlier Check¶

In [50]:
results = []
for col in column_numerical:
    # Calculate Q1 (25th percentile) and Q3 (75th percentile)
    Q1 = data[col].quantile(0.25)
    Q3 = data[col].quantile(0.75)
    
    # Calculate IQR
    IQR = Q3 - Q1
    
    # Determine lower and upper bounds
    lower_bound = Q1 - 1.5 * IQR
    upper_bound = Q3 + 1.5 * IQR
    
    # Identify outliers
    outliers = data[(data[col] < lower_bound) | (data[col] > upper_bound)]
    
    # Store results
    results.append({
        'Column': col,
        'Lower Bound': lower_bound,
        'Upper Bound': upper_bound,
        'Outlier Count': len(outliers),
        'Outlier Percentage (%)': (len(outliers) / len(data)) * 100,
    })

outlier_df = pd.DataFrame(results)
outlier_df

7 - Model Building¶

Functions for model evaluation¶

Function that return a dataframe with performance metrics (Accuracy, Recall, Precision and F1).

In [57]:
# defining a function to compute different metrics to check performance of a classification model built using sklearn
def model_performance_classification(model, predictors, target):
    """
    Function to compute different metrics to check classification model performance

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """

    # predicting using the independent variables
    pred = model.predict(predictors)

    acc = accuracy_score(target, pred)  # to compute Accuracy
    recall = recall_score(target, pred)  # to compute Recall
    precision = precision_score(target, pred)  # to compute Precision
    f1 = f1_score(target, pred)  # to compute F1-score

    # creating a dataframe of metrics
    df_perf = pd.DataFrame(
        {"Accuracy": acc, "Recall": recall, "Precision": precision, "F1": f1,},
        index=[0],
    )

    return df_perf

Function that returns the Confussion Matrix

In [58]:
def plot_confussion_matrix(model, predictors, target):
    """
    To plot the confusion_matrix with percentages

    model: classifier
    predictors: independent variables
    target: dependent variable
    """
    # Predict the target values using the provided model and predictors
    y_pred = model.predict(predictors)

    # Compute the confusion matrix comparing the true target values with the predicted values
    cm = confusion_matrix(target, y_pred)

    # Create labels for each cell in the confusion matrix with both count and percentage
    labels = np.asarray(
        [
            ["{0:0.0f}".format(item) + "\n{0:.2%}".format(item / cm.flatten().sum())]
            for item in cm.flatten()
        ]
    ).reshape(2, 2)    # reshaping to a matrix

    # Set the figure size for the plot
    plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))

    # Plot the confusion matrix as a heatmap with the labels
    sns.heatmap(cm, annot=labels, fmt="")

    # Add a label to the y-axis
    plt.ylabel("True label")

    # Add a label to the x-axis
    plt.xlabel("Predicted label")
In [59]:
def plot_confusion_matrices(models, predictors, target, title):
    """
    Plots confusion matrices for multiple models in a grid with 3 columns.
    
    Parameters:
    -----------
    models : list of tuples
        Each tuple is (model_name: str, model_object: classifier).
    predictors : pd.DataFrame or np.array
        Features (X_test or similar).
    target : pd.Series or np.array
        True labels (y_test or similar).
    """
    n_models = len(models)
    n_cols = 3
    n_rows = math.ceil(n_models / n_cols)  # Dynamic row calculation
    
    plt.figure(figsize=(6 * n_cols, 4 * n_rows))  # Scale figure size
    plt.suptitle(title, fontsize=18, fontweight='bold', y=1.02)
    
    for i, (name, model) in enumerate(models, 1):
        try:
            y_pred = model.predict(predictors)
            cm = confusion_matrix(target, y_pred)
            
            # Labels with counts + percentages
            labels = np.asarray(
                [[f"{item}\n{item/cm.sum():.2%}"] for item in cm.flatten()]
            ).reshape(2, 2)
            
            plt.subplot(n_rows, n_cols, i)
            sns.heatmap(cm, annot=labels, fmt="", cmap="Blues", cbar=False)
            plt.title(name)
            plt.ylabel("True label")
            plt.xlabel("Predicted label")
            
        except AttributeError:
            print(f"'{name}': Not a valid model.")
            continue
    
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

Model Evaluation Criterion¶

Defining scorer to be used for cross-validation and hyperparameter tuning¶

False Positives and False Negatives Are Equally Costly.

Both false positives and false negatives are highly costly in the certification process, and addressing either error is crucial:

  • False Positives: These occur when an applicant is predicted as Certified when, in reality, they should be Denied. This misclassification results in wasted time and resources throughout the application process. Moreover, it carries an opportunity cost by potentially displacing local talent or more qualified candidates, thereby depriving the workforce of their rightful contributions.
  • False Negatives: These occur when an applicant is predicted as Denied when they should be Certified. The consequence is the wrongful rejection of legitimate applicants, leading to unjust outcomes. Additionally, this error means the economy loses out on skilled labor, as candidates who could provide significant value to the workforce are not admitted.

The F1-score’s balance of precision (minimizing false positives) and recall (minimizing false negatives) ensures neither error disproportionately harms applicants or the labor market.

In [60]:
# Define F1 scorer for model evaluation
scorer = metrics.make_scorer(metrics.f1_score)

We are now done with pre-processing and evaluation criterion, so let's start building the model.

print("\n" "Cross-Validation Performance:" "\n")
for name, model in models:
    scoring = "f1"
    kfold = StratifiedKFold(
        n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=RS
    )  # Setting number of splits equal to 5
    cv_result = cross_val_score(
        estimator=model, X=X_train, y=y_train, scoring=scoring, cv=kfold
    )
    results.append(cv_result)
    names.append(name)
    
    print(f"{name}: {cv_result.mean()}")

print("\n" "Validation Performance:" "\n")

for name, model in models:
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    score = f1_score(y_val, model.predict(X_val))
    scores.append(score)
    print(f"{name}: {score}")
    results_scores_training.append(model_performance_classification(model, X_train, y_train))
    results_scores_validation.append(model_performance_classification(model, X_val, y_val))

Models with best performance¶

Decision Tree, Random Forest and Bagging have the worst scores with the original, oversample and undersample data. So this models are discarded for Hyper-parameter tuning.

All the models using undersampled data have a significant decrease in perfomance. So the undersample data will not be used for Hyper-parameter tuning.

The models that have the best performance (Highest F1 Score) are:

  • GBM with Original Data Cross-Val(0.8230), Validation Set(0.822)
  • AdaBoost with Original Data Cross-Val(0.8203), Validation Set(0.8175)
  • GBM with Oversample Data Cross-Val(0.8076), Validation Set(0.8132)
  • AdaBoost with Oversample Data Cross-Val(0.8013), Validation Set(0.8121)

The best XGBoost model is the one that uses the original data. With Oversample there is a slight decrease in performance.

  • XGBoost with Original Data Cross-Val(0.8095), Validation Set( 0.8074)

The best Undersample model is GBM:

  • GBM with undersample Data Cross-Val(0.7131), Validation Set(0.7641)

Overall GBM and AdaBoost are the best model with the original, oversample and undersample data. The best XGBoost and the best Undersample model will be added for Hyper-Parameter Tuning.

Hyperparameter Tuning¶

GBM with Oversampled Data - Tuning¶

In [87]:
%%time 
# Hyperparameter tuning for Gradient Boosting Classifier using RandomizedSearchCV
# Define the parameter grid for Gradient Boosting Classifier
param_grid = {
    # Core parameters
    'n_estimators': np.arange(50, 500, 50),          
    'learning_rate': [0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2],  
    'max_depth': np.arange(3, 11),                   
    'min_samples_split': np.arange(2, 21),           
    'min_samples_leaf': np.arange(1, 21),            
    
    # Stochastic gradient boosting (reduces overfitting)
    'subsample': [0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 1.0],              
    
    # Regularization
    'max_features': ['sqrt', 'log2', None],          
    'loss': ['log_loss', 'exponential'],             
}

# Initialize the Gradient Boosting Classifier
gbm_over = GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=RS)

# Perform Randomized Search with cross-validation
search_gbm_over = RandomizedSearchCV(
    estimator=gbm_over,
    param_distributions=param_grid,
    n_iter=50,                  
    cv=5,                       
    scoring='f1',          
    n_jobs=-1,                 
    random_state=RS
)

# Fit the model on the oversampled training data
search_gbm_over.fit(X_train_over, y_train_over)
print("Best parameters found: ", search_gbm_over.best_params_)
print("Best F1 score: ", search_gbm_over.best_score_)

%%time 
# Hyperparameter tuning for Gradient Boosting Classifier using RandomizedSearchCV
# Define the parameter grid for Gradient Boosting Classifier
param_grid = {
    # Core parameters
    'n_estimators': np.arange(50, 500, 50),          
    'learning_rate': [0.001, 0.01, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2],  
    'max_depth': np.arange(3, 11),                   
    'min_samples_split': np.arange(2, 21),           
    'min_samples_leaf': np.arange(1, 21),           
    
    # Stochastic gradient boosting (reduces overfitting)
    'subsample': [0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 1.0],              
    
    # Regularization
    'max_features': ['sqrt', 'log2', None],          
    'loss': ['log_loss', 'exponential'],             
}

# Initialize the Gradient Boosting Classifier
gbm_original = GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=RS)

# Perform Randomized Search with cross-validation
search_gbm_original = RandomizedSearchCV(
    estimator=gbm_original,
    param_distributions=param_grid,
    n_iter=50,                  # Number of parameter combinations to try
    cv=5,                       # 5-fold cross-validation
    scoring='f1',          # Use 'neg_mean_squared_error' for regression
    n_jobs=-1,                  # Use all CPU cores
    random_state=RS
)
# Fit the model with the training data
search_gbm_original.fit(X_train, y_train)
print("Best parameters found: ", search_gbm_original.best_params_)
print("Best F1 score: ", search_gbm_original.best_score_)

8 - Model Selection¶

GBM with the original dataset is the model with the best F1-Score. Nevertheless the XGBoost with Oversample is a very close second place. This two models will be compared performances with the test set. The test set represents unseen data, this set has not been used in any of the previous stages.

The Selected Model is GBM with the original training set.

9 - Actionable Insights and Recommendations¶

Facilitate the process of visa approvals.¶

  • The Gradient Boosting Model demonstrates an accuracy of 0.74, indicating strong overall performance. It generalizes effectively across training, validation, and test datasets, maintaining consistency in predictions.

  • The model excels in minimizing false negatives, ensuring that qualified applicants are rarely denied. This is reflected in its recall score of 0.89 on unseen data, highlighting its ability to correctly identify skilled employees.

  • However, the model exhibits a relatively higher incidence of false positives, increasing the likelihood of approving applicants who should have been denied. This is evident in its precision score of 0.76 on unseen data.

Recommended profile for the applicants for whom the visa should be certified or denied¶

Visa applicants with the following profile have a higher likelihood of visa certification:

  • Education: Higher education levels increase the probability of certification, particularly for applicants holding Master's or Doctorate degrees.
  • Job Experience: Applicants with previous professional experience are more likely to receive certification.
  • Prevailing Wage: Employees applying for positions with a prevailing wage above the median of $70,000 have a higher chance of certification.
  • Unit of Wage: Positions offering yearly wages are more commonly certified.
  • Continent: Applicants originating from Europe tend to have a greater likelihood of certification.
  • Region of Employment: Applicants seeking employment in the Midwest region are more frequently certified.

Visa applicants with the following characteristics are less likely to receive certification:

  • Education: Applicants who do not hold a degree face a higher probability of denial.
  • Work Experience: Lack of prior job experience significantly increases the likelihood of application rejection.
  • Wage Unit: Applications where the prevailing wage is expressed on an hourly basis are less likely to be approved.
  • Geographic Region: Applicants from South America, North America, and Oceania have a lower probability of certification.
